To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) perceived usefulness of a new system can be predicted by user evaluations of the system's requirements specifications, and (2) these evaluations can be made before the system is built, and thus before the system has been implemented in the workplace.

(1) preprototype user acceptance test measures of perceived usefulness are predictive of future workplace system usage, and (2) preprototype user tests of perceived ease of use are not predictive of future workplace use.

preprototype user acceptance assessments can be used for predictive purposes in software project management, provided that the assessments are based on perceived usefulness rather than perceived ease of use.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of when user acceptance testing of an information system should be done.
how user acceptance testing can be done much earlier than has traditionally been done.
how information systems can be better designed to fit the needs of their target users.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
preprototype usefulness assessments can be used in place of hands-on based usefulness assessments for the purposes of user acceptance testing, whereas preprototype ease of use assessments cannot.
preprototype user acceptance is possible, but not necessarily easy, and should be considered as a potential option for software project management, but not as a panacea.

the present findings suggest that preprototype user acceptance assessments can be used in conjunction with postprototype user acceptance assessments to provide a more comprehensive and accurate assessment of prospective system usage than would be possible based on postprototype assessments alone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
preprototype user acceptance measures of perceived usefulness are a valuable addition to the system development toolkit.

user acceptance testing can be done at a very early stage in the software development process, and that this can be done with a relatively small amount of resources and without the need for building a working prototype.

preprototype usefulness is an important and useful measure of user acceptance, but it should be supplemented by postprototype ease of use assessments to obtain the best possible predictions of future usage behavior after implementation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
preprototype user acceptance can be a powerful tool for improving the quality of new systems.

it is possible to predict future usage of a new system with high precision and accuracy based on user acceptance tests that can be done before building a working system prototype, which has significant implications for software project managers and developers who want to minimize costly errors in requirements specifications.
the conventional wisdom among information system developers that users must experience a working prototype before they can provide accurate assessments of the new system is only partially true.
